analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to test and report the harms of AI systems that decide jobs, loans, housing, and healthcare.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2025 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring companies above certain size thresholds to study any automated system they use to make critical decisions about people — in hiring, lending, housing, healthcare, education, utilities, and similar areas. Companies would have to test for biased or inaccurate results, consult outside stakeholders, try to fix identified harms, and file summary reports with the FTC, which would publish some information in a public, searchable repository. The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, and existing state laws would not be overridden.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose lives are shaped by automated systems — job applicants screened by algorithms, renters and borrowers scored by software, patients triaged by AI tools — gain a right to know these systems are tested for bias and error, plus a public registry of where such systems are used and how to contest decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People judged by automated decision systems

how_it_helps.text: Requires large companies to test whether their automated systems perform differently for people of different races, sexes, ages, disabilities, or incomes, and to document any negative impact and how they plan to fix it.

Covers decisions across nine major areas of life: education, employment, utilities, family planning, financial services, healthcare, housing, legal services, and other similarly consequential matters.
Directs the FTC to build a public, searchable repository of the automated decision systems in use, so consumers and researchers can see who is using what and how to contest a decision.
Requires companies to provide ways for consumers to contest, correct, appeal, or opt out of automated decisions, and to consult independent outside advocates and impacted communities.
Lets state attorneys general sue on residents' behalf and bars the bill from overriding stronger state laws.

analysis.who_pays: Larger companies that use or sell automated decision systems bear the cost of impact assessments, annual reporting, and potential FTC enforcement, and compliance costs may be passed to consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large companies using AI decision systems

drawbacks.text: The full impact assessments stay private: the bill only requires a summary report to the FTC, and it explicitly says companies need not disclose their assessments to the Commission or the public beyond that summary, limiting outside scrutiny.

The rules would take effect two years after being finalized, so real accountability could be several years away even if enacted, and the bill covers only larger companies, leaving small firms' automated systems unassessed.
Enforcement runs through the FTC and state attorneys general rather than individual lawsuits, so harmed consumers cannot sue directly under the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — forcing companies to find and fix biased or broken AI before it decides people's livelihoods — addresses a growing, largely invisible harm, and the bill is carefully scoped to large companies. The costs are real but modest: compliance paperwork, and the risk that assessments become a checkbox exercise whose findings stay secret. On balance the public gains more than it loses, though a stronger bill would require public disclosure of key findings rather than private filings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has not taken it up, so nothing has happened beyond that.

narrative.text: Wyden and seven Democratic colleagues introduced the bill on June 25, 2025.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, its only action since.
No committee markup, floor vote, or House action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies using automated decision systems are better off so far: no testing, reporting, or FTC oversight obligations have been imposed, and existing systems continue operating without documented scrutiny.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its impact-assessment framework for automated decision systems.

for.name: Sens. Warren, Booker, Heinrich, Lujan, Merkley, Hirono, and Schatz
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a seven-senator Democratic base of support.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 25, 2025 and has taken no further action on the bill, keeping it from any floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: They would face a new, ongoing duty to test and report on systems that decide hiring, lending, housing, and other critical outcomes, plus FTC enforcement for failures. Small companies below the size thresholds are exempt.

industries.industry: Credit scoring, HR screening, and tenant-screening data brokers
industries.note: Their products would face documented testing for discriminatory performance and public listing in an FTC repository. That raises costs but could also legitimize their use where systems pass review.
A new market for independent assessment, testing, and documentation work would arise from the bill's requirements.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to a Senate committee without bipartisan cosponsors or a markup never reach the floor; unless the Commerce Committee acts, this bill is likely to die at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
